How to generate a RESTful API request on Cisco Nexus Dashboard?
version:3.1.0
IP:192.168.11.33
API name: get nodes list
Parameter_fabricName:PEK-ACI

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends an HTTP GET request to retrieve a list of nodes associated with a specified fabric in a network. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to. The URL should include the target IP, API endpoint, and the fabricName query parameter placeholder https://<ip>/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/nodes?fabricName={fabricName}.

fabricName.description: The name of the fabric whose nodes are to be listed. This value is used to replace the {fabricName} placeholder in the URL.

message.content:
Below is a quick‑start guide that shows **two** ways to hit the “get nodes list” API from your Cisco Nexus Dashboard: | Method | What you’ll do | Example | |--------|----------------|---------| | **A – From the Nexus Dashboard UI** | 1️⃣ Log into the dashboard.
2️⃣ Go to *Developer → API Explorer* (or *Tools → API Explorer* depending on your UI layout).
3️⃣ In the drop‑down list pick **`get nodes list`**.
4️⃣ Fill in the required field `fabricName` with **`PEK-ACI`**.
5️⃣ Click **Execute** (or **Run**) and you’ll see the JSON response in the panel below. | ![UI screenshot](https://example.com/ui-explorer.png) *(replace with actual screenshot if you have one)* | | **B – Programmatically (Python)** | 1️⃣ Install the `requests` package (`pip install requests`).
2️⃣ Build the URL by inserting the IP and fabric name:
```python\nbase_ip = '192.168.11.33'\nfabric = 'PEK-ACI'\nurl = f'https://{base_ip}/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/nodes?fabricName={fabric}'\n```\n3️⃣ Add authentication – most Nexus APIs use Basic Auth or a bearer token. For Basic Auth you’d do:
```python\nauth = ('admin', 'cisco123') # replace with real creds\n```\n4️⃣ Make the GET request and pretty‑print the JSON:
```python\nimport requests, json\nresponse = requests.get(url, auth=auth, verify=False) # verify=False only if you’re okay with self‑signed certs\nprint(json.dumps(response.json(), indent=2))\n```\n5️⃣ Run the script (`python get_nodes.py`) and you’ll see the node list printed out. | ```bash\n$ python get_nodes.py\n{\n \"nodes\": [\n {\n \"nodeId\": \"10\",\n \"hostname\": \"leaf01.cisco.com\"\n },\n ...\n ]\n}\n``` | --- ### Quick‑reference for the function call (if you want to embed this in a larger automation framework) ```json { "name": "requests_get", "arguments": { "url": "https://192.168.11.33/sedgeapi/v1/cisco-nir/api/api/telemetry/flowrules/nodes?fabricName=PEK-ACI", "fabricName": "PEK-ACI" } } ``` When you pass this to the `functions.requests_get` tool, it will internally perform the same GET request as shown above. --- #### Things to keep in mind | Item | Detail | |------|--------| | **HTTPS & Certs** | The API uses HTTPS. If you’re hitting a lab device with a self‑signed certificate, either add `verify=False` in `requests`, or import the CA cert into your trust store. | | **Auth** | Most Nexus dashboards require authentication. Check whether the API expects Basic Auth, OAuth2 bearer tokens, or a custom header. | | **Rate limits / throttling** | The API may enforce per‑minute limits. If you’re automating many calls, add back‑off logic. | | **Error handling** | Always check `response.status_code`. A non‑200 status means something went wrong – inspect `response.text` for details. | That’s all there is to it! Once you’ve verified the call works from the UI, you can copy the same URL and parameters into your scripts or CI/CD pipelines. Happy automating!
